Crinia georgiana embryos undergo development within a gelatinous egg mass, with each individual egg containing approximately 70.2654 joules  of energy, an investment that sustains the yolk-dependent tadpole through its earliest stages. Following a period of sustained incubation at a stable temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the chorion ruptures after about 19 days , marking the hatching event. At this point of eclosion, the total energy content of the newly emerged larva is 65.5265 joules , reflecting the metabolic costs incurred during embryonic differentiation and the progressive yolk utilization that occurs within the jelly-coated egg. The newly hatched endotrophic tadpoles measure approximately 0.35 centimeters  in total length, a modest size typical of lecithotrophic larvae that have not yet commenced exogenous feeding. These pre-feeding tadpoles rely entirely on their remaining yolk reserves until the mouth opens and the trophic switch to active grazing begins.

The transition to exogenous feeding is accompanied by a measurable increase in dry mass, with newly hatched tadpoles weighing 0.00266 grams  immediately after eclosion. A separate estimate of dry weight at hatching, derived from a slightly different cohort, places this value at 0.00274 grams , suggesting minor inter-clutch variation in yolk provisioning. By the time the larval mouth is fully functional and first exogenous feeding commences, the free-swimming tadpoles have grown to a total length of 0.4 centimeters [Lb = 0.4 centimeters]. At this stage, the dry mass of the neonates, calculated from individuals sampled shortly after birth, is approximately 0.0029 grams , representing the combined contribution of residual yolk and the initial structural tissues laid down during organogenesis. These values are consistent with observations from other myobatrachid frogs, where small clutch components are offset by rapid early growth rates in the aquatic tadpole phase.

As Gosner-stage larvae progress through the pre-metamorphic phase, they accumulate somatic tissues steadily before the dramatic allometric shifts of metamorphic climax. At the point of metamorphosis, the total length of the transforming individual is approximately 0.6 centimeters , a value recorded from froglets undergoing tail resorption and limb development. The corresponding dry weight at this larval-juvenile transition is 0.02351 grams , reflecting the considerable mass gained during the herbivorous tadpole stage. The energy content of the metamorphosing larva at this critical juncture is 43.0153 joules , representing the net energetic capital available to support the terrestrial juvenile during the energetically expensive process of body plan reorganisation and skin keratinisation. This post-metamorphic juvenile, or froglet, then enters a period of rapid terrestrial growth, during which it must acquire sufficient resources to fuel both maintenance and the development of gonadal tissues.

The reproductive biology of Crinia georgiana has been examined under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 12 °C [T = 12 °C], reflecting the thermal regime typical of its southwestern Australian breeding season. Under these thermal conditions, females produce approximately 200 eggs over the course of a 365-day year [Ri = approximately 200 eggs over the course of a 365-day year], a maximum reproductive output consistent with the species' strategy of depositing multiple small clutches within a single breeding season. The age at birth, quantified as the time from oviposition to the onset of exogenous feeding, is 31 days [ab = 31 days] under the same thermal conditions at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This developmental timeline is slightly longer than that recorded for some tropical myobatrachids, likely reflecting the moderating influence of the cooler 12 °C [T = 12 °C] incubation environment on rates of embryonic differentiation and growth.

Puberty in Crinia georgiana, defined as the attainment of gonadal maturation and the onset of gametogenesis, occurs when individuals reach a total length of 2.2 centimeters [Lp = 2.2 centimeters], a size threshold that aligns closely with the body size at which reproductive maturation is observed in other small myobatrachid anurans. At this size, the corresponding dry weight of the maturing juvenile is approximately 0.20 grams , marking the transition from the sub-adult to the reproductively active adult stage. The asymptotic adult body size reaches 4.37 centimeters [Li = 4.37 centimeters] in total length and 1.2 grams  in dry weight, placing Crinia georgiana among the smaller members of its family. The first successful breeding event typically occurs 427 days after hatching [tR = 427 days after hatching] when maintained at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], a delay that reflects the time required to attain both the necessary body size and the energetic reserves needed for reproductive investment. Maximum recorded longevity under these captive conditions is 1825 days [am = 1825 days], placing this species at the moderately long-lived end of the spectrum for small Australian anurans at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C].
